meta.titre: Air and pollution: what air contains, its uses, and main pollutants
meta.sous_theme: Composition of air and air pollution

sections.contenu_markdown: On a dry-season afternoon in Douala, the air above a busy junction is full of smoke from motorcycle taxis, old generators and bush fires on the city edge. In the same city, hospitals depend on bottled oxygen for patients who cannot breathe well. Both situations come from the same air around us: a mixture of gases that is useful in some uses and harmful when polluted. The GCE O/L paper regularly asks about what air contains, how its gases are obtained, which gases pollute it, and what can be done about it.

items: A mixture can be separated by physical methods, because its parts are not chemically joined.
Combustion is burning a substance in oxygen.
Limewater turns milky when carbon dioxide is bubbled through it.
The boiling point is the temperature at which a liquid changes to a gas.

sections.titre: What air contains, how it is separated, and the main pollutants
sections.contenu_markdown:
**Air is a mixture of gases**, not a compound. Each gas keeps its own properties and can be separated by physical methods.

| Gas | Percentage of dry air (by volume) |
|---|---|
| Nitrogen | 78% |
| Oxygen | 21% |
| Argon and other noble gases | about 1% |
| Carbon dioxide | about 0.04% |

Air also contains a variable amount of **water vapour**.

**Fractional distillation of liquid air.** Air is filtered to remove dust, then compressed and cooled. Water vapour and carbon dioxide are removed first because they would freeze and block the pipes. The air is cooled further, to about $-200\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, until it is a liquid. The liquid air is then allowed to warm slowly in a fractionating column. The gases boil off at different temperatures: **nitrogen** ($-196\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$) boils first, then **argon** ($-186\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$), and **oxygen** ($-183\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$) last.

**Large-scale uses.** Nitrogen is used to make **ammonia** for fertilisers, and to freeze and preserve food. Oxygen is used in hospitals for patients, in welding and cutting metals, and in steel-making. Argon fills electric light bulbs.

**Tests.** Oxygen **relights a glowing splint**. Carbon dioxide turns **limewater milky**.

**Pollutants.** Combustion of fuels and bush burning release gases that harm health and the environment:

$\mathrm{C + O_{2} \rightarrow CO_{2}}$ (complete combustion)

$\mathrm{2C + O_{2} \rightarrow 2CO}$ (incomplete combustion, little oxygen)

$\mathrm{S + O_{2} \rightarrow SO_{2}}$ (burning sulphur in fuel)

$\mathrm{N_{2} + O_{2} \rightarrow 2NO}$ (in hot car engines)

variantes.quand_utiliser: When a question lists a pollutant and asks for its source or harm
variantes.contenu_markdown:
| Pollutant | Main source | Harm |
|---|---|---|
| Carbon monoxide | Incomplete combustion in engines, charcoal fires | Poisonous: it stops blood carrying oxygen |
| Sulphur dioxide | Burning fuels that contain sulphur, volcanoes | Acid rain, breathing problems |
| Oxides of nitrogen | Hot car engines, lightning | Acid rain, breathing problems |
| Carbon dioxide | Burning fuels, bush fires, deforestation | Greenhouse gas, global warming |
| Methane | Rotting waste, cattle | Greenhouse gas |
| Smoke and soot | Incomplete combustion | Lung damage, dirty surfaces |

**Remedies:** a catalytic converter in a car exhaust changes harmful gases to harmless ones, $\mathrm{2CO + 2NO \rightarrow 2CO_{2} + N_{2}}$. Power stations can remove sulphur dioxide with calcium oxide, $\mathrm{CaO + SO_{2} \rightarrow CaSO_{3}}$. Planting trees, ending bush burning and using cleaner fuels also help.

variantes.nom: Finding the percentage of oxygen in air
variantes.quand_utiliser: When a question describes copper heated in air in a gas syringe
variantes.contenu_markdown:
A known volume of air is pushed back and forth over **excess hot copper** between two gas syringes. The copper turns black as it takes oxygen from the air:

$\mathrm{2Cu + O_{2} \rightarrow 2CuO}$

When the apparatus has cooled to room temperature, the final volume is read. The loss in volume is the volume of oxygen.

$\%\ \text{oxygen} = \dfrac{\text{loss in volume}}{\text{original volume}} \times 100$

The result is close to 21%. The gas left is mostly nitrogen.

variantes.nom: Acid rain and the greenhouse effect
variantes.quand_utiliser: When the effect of a pollutant on the environment is asked
variantes.contenu_markdown:
**Acid rain.** Sulphur dioxide and nitrogen dioxide dissolve in rain water and form acids, for example $\mathrm{2SO_{2} + O_{2} + 2H_{2}O \rightarrow 2H_{2}SO_{4}}$ and $\mathrm{4NO_{2} + O_{2} + 2H_{2}O \rightarrow 4HNO_{3}}$. Acid rain corrodes iron roofs and bridges, dissolves limestone and marble buildings, harms trees and crops, and kills fish in lakes.

**Greenhouse effect.** Carbon dioxide and methane trap heat in the atmosphere, so the average temperature of the Earth rises (global warming). Effects include melting ice, rising sea level, droughts and floods.

sections.enonce_markdown: In an experiment, 80 cm$^3$ of dry air is passed back and forth over excess heated copper until the volume stops changing. After cooling to room temperature, the volume of gas is 63.2 cm$^3$. (a) Write an equation for the reaction. (b) Calculate the percentage of oxygen in the air sample. (c) Using 78% for nitrogen, find the volume of nitrogen and the volume of other gases in the 63.2 cm$^3$ that remain. (d) Explain why the copper must be in excess and why the apparatus must cool before the volume is read.

etapes.justification: Hot copper combines with oxygen to form black copper(II) oxide.

etapes.action: Find the volume of oxygen used.
etapes.justification: Only oxygen is removed, so the loss in volume is the oxygen.
Percentage = loss in volume divided by original volume, times 100.

etapes.resultat_markdown: $0.78 \times 80 = 62.4$ cm$^3$ of nitrogen; $63.2 - 62.4 = 0.8$ cm$^3$ of argon and other gases

etapes.justification: Excess copper ensures that all of the oxygen is used up. A hot gas has a larger volume than a cool gas.
etapes.resultat_markdown: The reading at room temperature gives a volume that can be compared fairly with the original volume.

sections.conclusion_markdown: The air contains **21% oxygen**; the remaining gas is **62.4 cm$^3$ of nitrogen** and **0.8 cm$^3$ of argon and other gases**.

items.pourquoi_faux: The two values are swapped. Nitrogen is the most abundant gas in the air.
items.correction_markdown: Air is about **78% nitrogen** and **21% oxygen**.

items.erreur_markdown: Air is a compound of nitrogen and oxygen.
items.pourquoi_faux: The gases in air are not chemically joined. Each keeps its own properties and they can be separated by physical methods.
items.correction_markdown: Air is a **mixture**, separated by fractional distillation of liquid air.

items.erreur_markdown: Carbon monoxide is made when fuel burns completely.
items.pourquoi_faux: Complete combustion in plenty of oxygen makes carbon dioxide. Carbon monoxide forms when the oxygen supply is limited.

items.erreur_markdown: Carbon dioxide is the main cause of acid rain.
items.pourquoi_faux: Acid rain is mainly caused by sulphur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen. Carbon dioxide is the main gas responsible for the greenhouse effect.
items.correction_markdown: Acid rain: sulphur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen. Global warming: carbon dioxide and methane.

items.enonce_markdown: (a) Give the approximate percentage by volume of nitrogen, oxygen and carbon dioxide in dry air. (b) Describe the test for oxygen and the test for carbon dioxide. (c) Name the process used to obtain nitrogen and oxygen from air.
items.solution_markdown: (a) Nitrogen **78%**, oxygen **21%**, carbon dioxide about **0.04%**. (b) Oxygen **relights a glowing splint**; carbon dioxide turns **limewater milky**. (c) **Fractional distillation of liquid air**, in which the gases separate because they have different boiling points.

items.enonce_markdown: A charcoal seller burns 1.2 g of pure carbon. ($A_r$: C = 12; O = 16; 1 mole of gas = 24 dm$^3$.) (a) Write the equation for complete combustion and calculate the volume and mass of carbon dioxide formed. (b) Write the equation for incomplete combustion and calculate the volume of oxygen needed in each case. (c) State why the incomplete combustion is more dangerous.
items.solution_markdown: (a) $\mathrm{C + O_{2} \rightarrow CO_{2}}$ $n(\mathrm{C}) = 1.2 / 12 = 0.10$ mol, so $n(\mathrm{CO_2}) = 0.10$ mol: volume $= 0.10 \times 24 = $ **2.4 dm$^3$** and mass $= 0.10 \times 44 = $ **4.4 g**. (b) $\mathrm{2C + O_{2} \rightarrow 2CO}$ Complete combustion needs 0.10 mol of $\mathrm{O_2}$, which is **2.4 dm$^3$**. Incomplete combustion needs half as much, 0.05 mol, which is **1.2 dm$^3$**. (c) Incomplete combustion makes **carbon monoxide**, a poisonous gas that stops the blood carrying oxygen.

items.enonce_markdown: A factory burns 16 g of sulphur in air. ($A_r$: S = 32; O = 16; Ca = 40; 1 mole of gas = 24 dm$^3$.) (a) Write the equation and calculate the volume of sulphur dioxide formed. (b) The gas is removed with calcium oxide, $\mathrm{CaO + SO_{2} \rightarrow CaSO_{3}}$ Calculate the mass of calcium oxide needed and the mass of calcium sulphite formed. (c) State two harmful effects of sulphur dioxide if it is released.
items.solution_markdown: (a) $\mathrm{S + O_{2} \rightarrow SO_{2}}$ $n(\mathrm{S}) = 16 / 32 = 0.50$ mol, so $n(\mathrm{SO_2}) = 0.50$ mol and $V = 0.50 \times 24 = $ **12 dm$^3$**. (b) The ratio is 1 : 1, so $n(\mathrm{CaO}) = 0.50$ mol. $M_r(\mathrm{CaO}) = 56$, so mass $= 0.50 \times 56 = $ **28 g**. $M_r(\mathrm{CaSO_3}) = 40 + 32 + 48 = 120$, so mass $= 0.50 \times 120 = $ **60 g**. (c) It causes **acid rain** (corroding roofs and buildings, harming trees and fish) and **breathing problems**.

items_markdown: Dry air is about **78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, 1% argon and other noble gases**, with a trace of carbon dioxide.
Air is separated by **fractional distillation of liquid air**; nitrogen boils off first, oxygen last.
Nitrogen is used for ammonia and fertilisers; oxygen for hospitals, welding and steel-making.
Carbon monoxide, sulphur dioxide, oxides of nitrogen, carbon dioxide and smoke are the main pollutants.
Acid rain comes from sulphur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen; global warming from carbon dioxide and methane.
